title: Mean People Fail: why benevolence beats meanness in startups
summary: Paul Graham argues that mean founders tend to fail because meanness makes you stupid, repels the best hires, and clashes with the benevolent drive that sustains great companies. As the games that matter shift from zero-sum control of scarce resources to building new things, the historical advantage of meanness is reversing.

principles.text: Fighting makes you stupid: wins come from case-specific tricks, not big ideas, so your brain spins its wheels.
principles.quote: One is that being mean makes you stupid. That's why I hate fights. You never do your best work in a fight, because fights are not sufficiently general.

principles.text: Startups win by transcending competitors, not attacking them. Race ahead instead of stopping to fight.
principles.quote: Startups don't win by attacking. They win by transcending. There are exceptions of course, but usually the way to win is to race ahead, not to stop and fight.

principles.text: Mean founders can't attract the best people, who have other options; top talent is critical for startups.
principles.quote: They can hire people who will put up with them because they need a job. But the best people have other options.

principles.text: Founders driven by improving the world outlast those driven by money, who take the early acquisition offer.
principles.quote: The ones driven by money take the big acquisition offer that nearly every successful startup gets en route. The ones who keep going are driven by something else.

principles.text: Success is shifting from zero-sum control of scarce resources to non-zero-sum building of new things, so meanness loses its edge.
principles.quote: Increasingly you win not by fighting to get control of a scarce resource, but by having new ideas and building new things.
